title: Mu
hook: a monk asks Zhaozhou whether a dog has Buddha-nature; he answers "mu" (Gateless Gate 1)

segments.voice: Yesterday: koan, and your line, don't solve it. Did you carry a puzzle for a while without forcing it? Day two hundred seventy-eight.

Northern China, more than a thousand years ago. A stray dog wanders through a monastery courtyard, the way stray dogs do. A monk watches it and turns to the old teacher Zhaozhou with a question he's clearly been saving. Does a dog have Buddha-nature, or not? The case doesn't say why he asks. But every monk there knew what the books said, so it's a question with a trap in it. Zhaozhou gives him one syllable. Wu. In Japanese, mu. It's the first case in the Gateless Gate, and for centuries it's been the first koan many Zen students are given.
screen: `A STRAY DOG IN THE COURTYARD.` → `DOES IT HAVE BUDDHA-NATURE?` → `ONE SYLLABLE.`

segments.voice: Here's why the answer is so strange. Mahayana sutras teach that all living beings have Buddha-nature, the capacity to wake up. Every monk in that courtyard knew it. So the textbook answer is yes. And mu means no. Or not. Or without. Or nothing. Zhaozhou just contradicted the scriptures, it seems, in one breath. That's the hook the koan sets. If you argue that he meant no, you're stuck. If you argue that he meant yes, you're stuck. Wumen, the monk who compiled the Gateless Gate in 1228, says in his comment that mu isn't the no of yes and no, and it isn't the nothing of being and nothing. He tells students to work on it with their whole body, day and night, like someone who has swallowed a red-hot iron ball and can't spit it out. Tradition says Wumen himself worked on mu for six years. There's another detail most people never hear. In a different collection, the Book of Serenity, the same question comes to Zhaozhou on another day, and that time he answers: yes. Many teachers read it as a sign that the answer was never the point. What the teacher cared about was what was happening in the person who asked. Zhaozhou, by tradition, lived to about one hundred twenty, teaching into extreme old age, famous for plain words that stopped people in their tracks. Mu is his most famous one. Students don't explain it. They become it, breath by breath.
screen: `ALL BEINGS HAVE BUDDHA-NATURE.` · `MU: NO, NOT, NOTHING.` · `A RED-HOT IRON BALL.` · `ON ANOTHER DAY, YES.` · then, large: `MU.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. On each out-breath, let the sound mu go out with it, silently, or as the softest hum. Mu. Not thinking about what it means. Just the sound, riding the breath all the way out. When a thought comes, let it be followed by the next mu. If you'd like, imagine the sound filling the whole body, head to feet. The bell holds the time.
Mu. Zhaozhou's one-syllable answer about the dog: no, not, nothing, and none of those. The first koan of the Gateless Gate.
Your line: mu. Today, when you catch yourself stuck between yes and no, breathe mu once, and see what's there before you pick a side. Day two hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: In Rinzai Zen and some Western Zen communities, 'mu' is often the first koan a teacher assigns; students breathe with it in sitting meditation and bring their response to private interviews with the teacher.

match.prompt: match each piece of the first koan.

myth: Zhaozhou's 'mu' simply means dogs lack Buddha-nature
Wumen says it isn't the no of yes and no.
Mahayana sutras teach that all beings have Buddha-nature
that's why the monk's question was a trap.
in another collection Zhaozhou answers the same question with yes
the Book of Serenity records both answers.

fork.setup: you're Zhaozhou. a monk asks whether a dog has Buddha-nature, a question he already knows the textbook answer to. what do you say?
options: quote the sutra: yes, all beings have it.
give a long talk on Buddha-nature.
fork.reveal: Zhaozhou said 'wu', mu in Japanese, which cut off both the textbook yes and any clever no.

original.note: Japanese mu, Chinese wú: no, not, without, nothing.

trapdoor: what you thought: mu means 'no', so the answer is no.
what it means: a word that cuts off both yes and no, held in practice rather than explained.

what a scholar hears: the 'yes' version is in the Book of Serenity, case 18, and Dahui Zonggao's huatou ('critical phrase') method in the twelfth century made 'wu' the favorite koan before Wumen placed it first.

sources.ref: Gateless Gate (Wumenguan), case 1 and Wumen's comment

notes: Koan and Wumen's comment paraphrased (red-hot iron ball image).
'Tradition says Wumen worked on mu for six years': confirm source.
Zhaozhou's traditional lifespan (778–897, about 120 years): given as tradition.
Trapdoor: Dahui's promotion of 'wu' as a hwadu before 1228: confirm.
Stray dog 'wandering through the courtyard' is scene-setting; the case itself gives no setting. Keeper may prefer to trim.
Audit 2026-09-30: hook no longer invents the monk's motive; 'scholars point to it' changed to 'many teachers read it'; trapdoor uses the Chinese huatou (hwadu is the Korean term) for Dahui.
